title: An Execution-Oriented Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Simulate→Rollback Pipelines for LLM‑Assisted NetOps: a Confirmatory Study with gpt-5‑mini
abstract: We evaluate whether an execution‑oriented pipeline that augments LLM configuration generation with deterministic validation, simulator enactment, and automatic rollback (pipeline C) reduces actionable misconfigurations relative to a generation‑only baseline (pipeline A). Following a preregistered paired design (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1), we applied gpt‑5‑mini to N=160 vendor‑neutral NetOps tasks (routing, ACL, NAT) and measured an actionable misconfiguration label produced by a deterministic simulator. All design choices, seeds, validators, and artifacts were frozen before execution. Results: both baseline and guarded (pipeline C) conditions produced 0 actionable misconfigurations in the confirmatory task set (paired difference = 0.00, 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00], McNemar exact p=1.0). Interpretation: within this task corpus and tooling, the generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline did not lower actionable misconfiguration rates because the baseline generation outputs were already non‑actionable under the simulator checks (ceiling effect). We present the confirmed preregistration, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts, discuss threats to validity, and recommend harder task sets, multi‑model evaluation, and richer validators for future work.

sections.introduction: Generative models and agentic LLMs are increasingly proposed to assist NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and limited self‑healing. Prior work highlights two core risks: fluent but unsafe configuration output (hallucination) and unclear operational assurance when model output is enacted on real devices [VeriFlow 2012; Mondal et al. 2023; MeshAgent 2025]. This study asks a narrowly scoped, preregistered confirmatory research question: Does an execution‑oriented pipeline that combines generation, deterministic validation, simulator enactment, and automatic rollback (pipeline C) reduce the actionable misconfiguration rate by ≥30% relative to a generation‑only baseline (pipeline A)? Our contribution is a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed execution of that comparison using a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), with all prompts, seeds, validators, simulator, and analysis frozen and published.
sections.related_work: We position this work among three lines. (1) Real‑time/verifier‑assisted synthesis and checking for network configurations (VeriFlow [Khurshid et al., 2012]; subsequent data‑plane verifiers and incremental update tools). (2) LLM‑for‑NetOps studies that pair generation with constraint/validator machinery (e.g., MeshAgent [Zhou et al., 2025]; Rajdeep Mondal et al., 2023 on verified prompt programming). (3) AIOps/NetOps benchmark efforts that emphasize task realism and execution (OpsEval and related suites). Unlike purely capability benchmarks, our focus is operational: measured enactability as judged by a deterministic simulator and a concrete paired hypothesis test under a frozen preregistration.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and experimental design: We preregistered the full plan (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) before execution. Design: paired confirmatory comparison (baseline vs guarded) on N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks split into routing (≈64), ACL (≈64), and NAT/other (≈32) clusters. Model and prompting: single model gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API), single initial generation call per task, up to one repair call per task when allowed by the frozen pipeline. Guarded pipeline (C): generation → constraint/validator check → simulator enactment → automatic rollback scoring. Baseline (A): generation only (same initial prompt) with simulator scoring of generated config but without in‑pipeline validation or pre‑enactment rollback. Data selection and exclusions: only public/synthetic vendor‑neutral tasks; duplicates and near‑duplicates were excluded per preregistered hashing and similarity rules. Metrics and primary estimand: per‑task binary actionable misconfiguration label from the deterministic simulator; primary estimand = paired difference in actionable misconfiguration proportion (A − C). Analysis plan: paired bootstrap (10,000 replicates) for 95% CIs and exact McNemar test for paired binary outcomes; secondary, cluster‑specific descriptive analyses and validator operational metrics. Reproducibility: all prompts, seeds, canonicalizers, simulator, and analysis scripts were archived; execution and analysis manifests (paths and hashes) are published with the artifacts.
sections.results: Execution summary: run completed per preregistration (execution_manifest). Model calls used: 160 (one shared initial generation per task), completed episode pairs: 160, failed episodes: 0. Primary confirmatory outcome: baseline actionable proportion = 0/160 (0.00). Guarded actionable proportion = 0/160 (0.00). Contingency: n11=160 (both safe), n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference (A−C) = 0.00; bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). McNemar exact two‑sided p=1.00. Secondary analyses: no discordant pairs to analyze by cluster; validator block rates and false‑positive rates are reported in the artifact logs (none materially impacted the confirmatory set). All principal numeric outputs match published analysis artifacts (hashes in the execution manifest).
sections.discussion: The preregistered hypothesis (≥30% relative reduction) is not supported; the observed paired difference is exactly zero. The most parsimonious interpretation is a ceiling effect: the chosen confirmatory task set and canonicalized prompt yielded generation outputs that the deterministic simulator judged non‑actionable under its formalized safety checks. Possible reasons: (i) tasks were too small/benign for the chosen model and prompt; (ii) the simulator’s safety predicate focused on a narrow class of actionable faults and may miss other operational risks; (iii) a single‑model evaluation limits generality. Operational implication: when baseline generation already meets the simulator’s enactability checks, additional guarded infrastructure provides no measured reduction in the operational metric; however, this does not imply equivalence in harder, more realistic deployments. We publish raw traces to allow others to re‑score with alternative validators or simulators.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired comparison of a generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline against a generation‑only baseline using gpt‑5‑mini across 160 confirmatory NetOps tasks. The confirmatory result was null: both conditions produced zero actionable misconfigurations under the chosen deterministic simulator and safety checks. The null outcome highlights the importance of (i) task difficulty calibration, (ii) multi‑model and multi‑validator assessments, and (iii) deployment‑level realism when evaluating agentic NetOps pipelines. We release the full preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts to support follow‑on studies that address these limitations.

limitations: Confirmatory task set produced a ceiling effect (baseline generation judged non‑actionable by the simulator), limiting the ability to measure pipeline C’s benefit.
Single model (gpt‑5‑mini) — results do not generalize to other foundation models or model sizes.
Deterministic simulator and safety predicate are an abstraction of operational risk and may not capture all real‑world failure modes (external validity).
Public/synthetic vendor‑neutral tasks; no live device enactment or production telemetry was used.
Potential contamination risk from model training data overlap with public corpus was checked per preregistered hashing/similarity rules, but residual overlap cannot be fully excluded.
Sample size (N=160) was chosen per pre‑registered power calculations; detectable effects near the preregistered target depend on baseline rate assumptions and task difficulty.
